10. The Land Acquisition Act of 1894, which is the primary legislation governing land acquisition in Pakistan, has its roots in earlier laws established during the British colonial period. The historical background of this legislation can be traced back to the Bengal Regulation of 1824, which was the first piece of legislation in India regarding the Page-7 -of22 acquisition ofproperty. This regulation aimed to provide rules for govemment officers to obtain land or other immovable property at a fair valuation. The Land Acquisition Act of 1894 was enacted to consolidate and amend the laws relating to the acquisition of land for public purposes and to provide for the payment of compensation to the persons interested in such land. The Act was desigrred to facilitate the acquisition of land for various public projects, including infrastructure development, urban planning, a16 other governmental initiatives. It established a framework for the process of land acquisition, including the notification process, assessment of compensation, and the rights of landowners. Over the years, the Act has undergone several amendments to address various issues and to align with changing socio-economic conditions. For instance, the provisions regarding compensation have been a focal point of contention, leading to judicial interpretations and modifications in the practice. The Act's application has been challenged in various cases, highlighting the need for fair compensation and adherence to principles of natural justice during the acquisition process. The Land Acquisition Act of 1894 emerged from a historical context of colonial land policies and has evolved through legislative amendments and judicial scrutiny to address the complexities ofland acquisition in Pakistan. The principles established by the apex court for determining compensation for acquired land are not often adhered to, leading to prolonged litigations Page-8-of22 that incur significant costs to the national exchequer. Section 23 of the Land Acquisition act, 1894 provides elaborate guidelines for determination of amount of compensation of the acquired land that are to be considered at the time of fixation of compensation. Wisdom in this regard is sought from the case law reported as "Malik Tariq lvlahmood and others Vs. Prwince of Pmjab and others" (2023 SCMR 102). Mode of determtning the compensation of acquired land is provided in section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which depicts that the landowner is entitled to compensation and not just market value, as such, any loss or tniury occastoned by its severing from other property of the landowner, by change of residence or place of business and loss of pro/its are also relevant factors.

While conducting said exercise, oral evidence, iffound credible and reltable can also be taken into consideration. The requirement of Article 71 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, sqtnrely requires that it should be produced directly if the same is in oral form.

Before proceeding further, it would be in order to reproduce the relevant provision of Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which reads as under: - "23. Matters to be considered in determining compensotion. (1) In determining the amount of compensation to be awarded fo, land acquired under this Act, the Court shall take into consideration: First, the market'value of the land at the date of the publication of the noti/ication under section 4, subsection (I).
7. This provision stands amended by the NWFP Amendment Ordinance XVil of 2001 in the following terms:- "First, the market value of the land on the date of taking possession of the land."

13. While determining compensation under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the courts are required to adopt a considerate and sympathetic approach when adjudicating the claims of individuals whose property has been compulsorily acquired by the State against their will for public purposes. Reliance in this regard is placed on the judgment reported as "National Highway Authority vs. Rai Ahmad Nawaz Khan and others" (2023 SCMR 700). Relevant excerpt from paragraph 8 of the said judgment is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

8. It is important to state that the intention of the legislature behind section 23 was that whenever a n a Page-16-of22 Court is determining the quantum of compensation to be au,arded to those who had been subjected to exercise of the power of eminent domain under the LAA 1894, it needs to be considerate and sympathetic towards the claims made by those whose property was compulsortly taken by the state against their will for a public purpose. Section 23 allows a Court to cornpensate such landowners for giving up their properties for the greater good, on the doctrine of individual rights must tve way to the greater public interest (salwpopuli suprema lexesto).

14. Before proceeding further, it is essential to address a pertinent legal question: whether the Referee court or this Court in appellate jurisdiction can enhance the compensation beyond the amount specifically claimed by the landowners in their reference appltcations? The answer to this question is firmly rooted in the principles of justice and statutory interpretation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The august Supreme Court of Pakistan, in its authoritative pronouncement reported as "Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Defence, Ranalpindi Military Estates Officer, Hazara Circle, Abbottabad ond another v. Itht. Ayesha Bibi (widow) and others" (2024 SCMR 1323) has conclusively held that the Referee Court may enhance compensation beyond the amount claimed in the reference application, provided that the evidence produced by the parties justifies such enhancement in accordance with Section 23 of the Act. Paragraphs 12 and 13 of the said judgment categorically state that the landowners, whose property has Page'17 - of22 been taken through the exercise of eminent domain, are entitled to fair market value, and that strict adherence to procedural safeguards undet Sections 9 and 25 of the Act is vital. Furthermore, it was emphasized that faimess demands compensation not be arbitrarily capped by the originally claimed amount if the evidence reveals a higher valuation' The Supreme Court thus held:

"...in cases, where there is a faihtte of strict compliance of the said provisions of the Act, and in particular Sections 9 and 25, then the Referee Cotrt may proceed to adiudge the compensation for the acquired property beyord the amount claimed by the landowners in the reference applications, if the evidence produced by the parties iustify such enlwncenent in accordance with Section 23 of the Act..."

15. As an appeal is a continuation of the original proceedings, the High Court is comPetent to apply the procedural and substantive provisions governing the original proceedings by invoking Sections 53 and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 r/w 5.107(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. In view of the above legal position, the Referee Court, and this Court in appellate jurisdiction, has the lawful authority to award compensation in excess of the amount claimed by the landowners, where the record and evidence on file support such an enhancement. Any objection to this enhancement merely on the ground of being beyond the initial claim amount is thus devoid of legal merit. a Page-18-of22 16. The learned Referee Court declined to award 60/o interest on the compensation amount on the gfound that the relevant provision had been deleted from the statute book. However, in view of the latest amendment to Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, it is evident that the award of 6% simple interest has not been deleted. For better understanding, the amended Section 28 is reproduced below, which reads as follows:

Section. 28: Collector may be direcled to pay interest on occess compensation.- If the sum which, in the opinion of the Court, the collector ought to have awarded as compensation is in excess of the sum whtch the Collector did mvard as compensation, the nvard of the Court may direct that the Collector shall [deposit with the court such amount as determined by itJ. (K.P.K Amendmentt 17. In section 28, for the words "pay interest on such excess at the rate of six per centum per annum from the date on which he took possession of the land to the date of payment of such excess into Court," the words "deposit with the Court such amount as determined by it" shall be substituted. By virtue of amendment to section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1984, as made by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa legislature, the phrase pertaining to the payment of interest on the excess amount @ Rs. 6%owas deleted, however, under the amended provision, the Collector is required to deposit the excess amount as determined by the Referee Court, before the court. If the excess amount is deposited in accordance with a\ .-a w Page-19-of22 the amended provision, no interest shall be levied on such amount. Conversely, in the event of failure, on the part of the Land Acquisition Collector or the acquiring department to deposit the excess amount before the Referee Court, they may not be absolved of their liability to pay interest on the said amount. No doubt, the award of interest under section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act,1894 is discretionary in nature and the Court may exercise such discretion judiciously, while passing an appropriate order. However, section 34 of Land Acquisition Act, 1894 as amended by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa legislature, provides that where the amount of compensation is not paid or deposited on or before the taking possession of the land, the Collector shall be liable to pay the amount awarded amount along with simple interest at the rate of 6Yo per annum from the date of taking possession, until the amount is so paid or deposited. The language employed in the amended section 34 is mandatory in nature obligating the Collector to pay compensation along with interest to be calculated from the date of taking possession until the final payment or deposit of the excess amount is made. In the award, it is specifically admitted that the acquiring department took possession of the acquired land on 24-04-2009 and the parties are not in dispute on this point. Although, section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 has been amended by the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the amendment did not delete the provision for payment of 6Yo A a Page-20-of22 simple interest. Under the amended law, the Collector remains bound to pay 60/o interest on the amount of compensation determined by the court which exceeds the amount already deposited. In the present case, while the collector is not liable to pay 6% simple interest on the portion of compensation already deposited in court, he is obligated to pay 60/o simple interest on the amount adjudged by the court to be in excess of the initial deposit. Guidance in this regard is derived from the case law reported as "Nawabzada Abdul Qadir Khan and others Vs. Land Acqutsition Collector, Mardan and others". (2023 SCMR 950). Para 7 of the judgment supra reads as under;

7. Corning to the points raised by the Additional Afuocate Generals fo, KP, we note that section 34 of the LAA 1894 has never been repealed by the KP Provincial Assembly, and therefore have no qualms in arriving at the conclusion that the imposition of sixpercent interest imposed by both the Courts had been done in accordance with lan. To that extent, the Additional Advocate Generals, KP hatte not been able to point out any illegality in the imposition of the six per cent interest by both the Courts below. Section 34 of the LAA 1894 still holds the Jield and continues to do so. It is, however, important to clarify that unlike riba/interest that accrues out of a /inancial obligation between the parties, the word "interest" in section 34 of the LAA 1894 is not interest strictosensu. The interest awarded to landowners under section 34 is compensatory in nature that allows the Court to compensate the landowners for the financial loss landowners would suffer from the date of acquisition n ,-)

V Page-21-of22 till payment of compensation by the acquiring authority. Unlike a /inanctal transaction, where parttes are often assumed to be equal in bargaining power and are deemed to be consenting to a transaction, an exercise of eminent domain cannot in any sense be construed as either a consenting transaction between the parties involved (i.e. the State and the landowners) nor can it be assumed by any stretch of imagination that the state and the landowners are equal in terms of bargaining power. Emtnent domain is, after all, a unilateral power of the government and no consent from the affected landowners is required under the law before the state can exercise eminent domain under the LAA 1894. Even otherwise, as held by this Court in the case of Shetkh Muhammad Ilyos Ahmed v. In light of the foregoing discussion, it is held that the findings of the learned Referee Court warrant interference in exercise of appellate jurisdiction; Accordingly, the appeals of the objectors/landowners are partially allowed and the impugned judgments and decrees are modified to the extent that the compensation for the acquired land is fixed at the rate of Rs. 6,00,000/- (six lac) per Kanal.
